title: The heart in twins: twin-twin transfusion

items.question: Which twin pregnancies are at risk of twin-twin transfusion syndrome?
options: Monochorionic twins
All twin pregnancies equally
Dichorionic twins only
Only twins with a heart defect
items.explanation: AHA 2014 reported that the syndrome occurs in about 10% to 20% of monochorionic twin pregnancies. This is a historical estimate, not a current prognosis.

items.question: Which cardiac findings are often seen in the recipient twin?
options: Ventricular dysfunction, chamber enlargement, hypertrophy and atrioventricular valve regurgitation
A normal heart in almost every case
Small ventricles with thin walls
Isolated pericardial effusion and nothing else
items.explanation: These are the recipient's usual findings. Right ventricular outflow abnormalities can also develop.

items.question: What is true of Quintero staging?
options: It is widely used but does not include cardiac findings
It is based on the fetal echocardiogram
It has been replaced by the Cincinnati score
It predicts outcome from cardiac findings
items.explanation: Quintero staging is the most used system and has no cardiac component. Cardiac scores have been proposed.

items.question: Do cardiac findings reliably predict outcome in twin-twin transfusion?
options: That is controversial
Yes, in all cases
No, they never do
Only in the donor twin
items.explanation: AHA 2014 calls the value of cardiac findings for predicting outcome controversial.

items.question: After laser treatment, what does AHA 2014 say about the surviving twins?
options: Consider a fetal echocardiogram 24 to 48 hours later
A fetal echocardiogram is never needed
Repeat the study only at birth
Repeat the study after 2 weeks
items.explanation: AHA 2014 suggests that a fetal echocardiogram 24 to 48 hours after laser treatment should be considered. Confirm against the current fetal therapy protocol.
